adjudications.justification: The invoice contains 40 consignments for the calendar month in question, far exceeding the "more than 12 consignments" threshold in §5, and this count is identical (40) under all three candidate date bases (invoice document, booking date, ship date). Because every basis agrees, the rate card's noted ambiguity about which date defines the calendar month (alpine-express.md §5) does not actually affect the outcome here — the invoice qualifies for the 5% volume incentive discount on any reading. The carrier's declared discount amount is stated as zero, which is not supported by §5 given this clear qualification. This is a determinable entitlement failure: the carrier owed a discount and did not apply one. That said, one line on this invoice is not yet pricing-determined, so the exact discount shortfall in rupee terms cannot be finalized until that line is resolved — the dispute here is on entitlement, not on a computed shortfall figure.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Alpine invoice ALPINE-0726 covers 40 consignments for the month, but the carrier's invoice reflects no volume incentive discount applied.
memo_narrative.why: Under §5, tendering more than 12 consignments in a calendar month entitles the customer to a 5% discount on that invoice's total; the 40-consignment count holds under every possible date basis, so the lack of any discount is not supported by the contract, even though one line's pricing is still pending and affects the final discount figure.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Request a corrected invoice from Alpine applying the §5 volume incentive discount, noting that the exact discount figure should be finalized once the one outstanding line on this invoice is priced.

adjudications.justification: Consignment FF-8003, tied to a single shipment (SH-4003), appears as a full freight line on two separate Falcon invoices (FALCON-2026-07A and FALCON-2026-07B), each individually priced correctly against the contract's per-km, weight-banded base freight (§1) plus applicable fuel surcharge (§3) for this 900 kg, 275 km, standard-service shipment with no special handling. The contract's freight schedule charges a consignment once for its carriage; nothing in the shipment record, invoice evidence, or contract (e.g. no re-delivery, correction, or split-shipment indicator) explains a legitimate second charge for the same consignment note. Absent such an explanation, the second occurrence is an unsupported duplicate charge that should not be paid twice.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Falcon billed consignment FF-8003 (shipment SH-4003) as a full freight line on two separate invoices, 07A and 07B, with identical amounts and no indication of a re-delivery, correction, or split shipment.
memo_narrative.why: The contract's freight charges (§1) are for carriage of a given consignment, and §5 confirms no charges beyond the agreed schedule are payable without prior written agreement; a second, unexplained full charge for the same consignment is not supported by the contract or the shipment record.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Raise this as a duplicate-billing dispute with Falcon within the 45-day window (§7), asking them to confirm which invoice (07A or 07B) is the valid billing for FF-8003 and to withdraw or credit-note (§8) the duplicate.

adjudications.justification: Clause 3 fixes the fuel surcharge at a flat 12% of the freight charge (base freight plus express premium), with no variable rate or carrier discretion. Falcon's own credit note FALCON-CN-01 admits the invoice applied 15% "in error" and states the contractual rate is 12%, which corroborates the independently-determined line-level pricing delta for FF-8005 (already computed as a dispute at the line level via du:line:FALCON-2026-07A:FF-8005). This is not a case of contract ambiguity — §3's 12% rate is stated plainly and the carrier's own correction confirms the same reading — so the underlying billing error is well established. Because the credit note amount matches the already-counted line delta exactly, this finding contributes no new dispute amount; it simply corroborates the existing line-level dispute.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Falcon applied a 15% fuel surcharge on consignment FF-8005 instead of the contractual 12% rate, and later issued its own credit note (FALCON-CN-01) acknowledging the error.
memo_narrative.why: Clause 3 fixes the fuel surcharge at 12% of the freight charge with no exceptions, and Falcon's own credit note confirms the 15% figure was billed in error, so this is a clear, carrier-admitted overcharge rather than a matter of interpretation.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: No separate action needed on this credit note beyond confirming it is applied against the already-flagged line-level dispute for FF-8005 on invoice FALCON-2026-07A; do not treat it as an additional deduction.

adjudications.justification: The consignment's chargeable weight (after the §1 floor is applied) is exactly 50.0 kg. §2 defines the per-kg rate for "under 50 kg" and "over 50 kg" using strict inequalities, leaving exactly 50 kg covered by neither band. This is not a computational error but a genuine gap in the rate card itself -- the carrier's own structured rate card explicitly flags this exact scenario as an unresolved ambiguity. Nothing elsewhere in the contract (service level, handling, volume incentive, or invoicing clauses) supplies a tie-breaking rule for the boundary weight, so there is no basis to pick either the 9.50 or 8.25 per-kg rate without guessing. Per policy, a genuine rate-band gap of this kind must not be resolved by selecting a band that isn't actually written in the contract, so this requires a human ruling rather than an accept or dispute call.

memo_narrative.what_happened: This consignment's chargeable weight came out to exactly 50 kg, which sits precisely on the boundary between Alpine's two freight rate bands.
memo_narrative.why: Per §2, the contract sets the per-kg rate for consignments "under 50 kg" and "over 50 kg" using strict less-than/greater-than language, so a weight of exactly 50 kg is not clearly covered by either rate -- the contract itself does not state a rate for this boundary case.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Escalate to Alpine Express's account manager for a ruling on which per-kg rate applies to consignments at exactly 50 kg, and request that future contract language or an amendment close this gap.

adjudications.justification: The pricing trace correctly applies the contract: consignment FF-8005 (SH-4005) has a billed weight of 260 kg, which falls squarely in the "up to and including 500 kg" band at ₹18.00/km (§1), over a booked distance of 800 km, giving a base freight of 14,400. The express service premium of 15% on base freight (§2) and the 12% fuel surcharge on base-plus-express (§3) are both correctly computed and compounded in the order the contract specifies, yielding an expected freight charge that is fully reconciled from the shipment facts and rate card with no unresolved band boundary, no missing accessorial trigger (special_handling is empty, so residential delivery under §4 correctly did not fire), and no ambiguity in weight banding (260 kg is not near the 500/501 kg boundary noted as ambiguous elsewhere in this rate card). The billed amount exceeds this correctly-traced expected amount by a determinable margin, which is a straightforward overcharge relative to the contract's own freight formula rather than a defensible alternate reading of any clause.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Falcon billed consignment FF-8005 above the amount the contract's freight formula (base per-km rate by weight band, plus express premium and fuel surcharge) produces for this 260 kg, 800 km, express shipment.
memo_narrative.why: The weight band, express premium, and fuel surcharge are each correctly and unambiguously determined under §1, §2, and §3, with no boundary or trigger ambiguity for this consignment, so the amount above the contract-derived figure is an unsupported overcharge.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Raise a billing dispute with Falcon citing §1-§3 and request a corrected invoice for FF-8005 reflecting the contract-derived freight charge.

adjudications.justification: The shipment record shows 700 kg billed weight and 800 km distance, standard service, no special handling. Recomputing under the contract: 700 kg falls squarely in the 501-2,000 kg band (§1) at ₹24/km, giving base freight for 800 km; the express premium (§2) correctly does not fire since service_level is standard, not express; the 12% fuel surcharge (§3) applies to the base freight only. No accessorial applies since special_handling is empty (§4). This reconstruction matches the pipeline's expected_amount exactly and is not near any contract boundary ambiguity (700 kg is well inside the 501-2,000 band, not near the 500/501 kg gap noted in the rate card's ambiguities). The billed amount exceeds this correctly-derived figure, and §5's whitelist means no other accessorial or charge is payable absent a prior written rate confirmation, none of which is evidenced here. This is a clear, determinable overcharge.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Falcon billed consignment FF-8011 (700 kg, Mumbai-Bengaluru, 800 km, standard service) above the amount that the contract's base freight and fuel surcharge formula supports.
memo_narrative.why: Recomputing base freight under §1's 501-2,000 kg band and the §3 fuel surcharge on top reproduces a lower figure than billed, with no applicable express premium (§2) or accessorial (§4) to explain the gap, and §5 bars any other uncontracted charge.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Request a corrected invoice from Falcon Freight for FF-8011 citing §1 and §3, and raise the dispute within the 45-day window under §7.

adjudications.justification: The pricing trace cleanly reconstructs the contracted freight for this consignment under §1: a weight component (60kg billed weight × ₹6/kg) plus a distance component (85km × ₹2/km), summing to the expected amount. The shipment record shows no special_handling entries, so the cold chain premium in §3 correctly does not fire (consistent with the trace showing it as not fired). No accessorials or other surcharges appear anywhere in the evidence to explain the gap between the billed amount and the contract-derived figure. The only ambiguity noted on this rate card concerns whether 'booked lane distance' in §1 differs from a shipment's actual distance_km, but only a single distance value (85km, matching the shipment record) appears anywhere in the evidence — there is no second, competing distance figure that would make this an unresolved two-readings situation for this specific consignment. With no contractual basis identified for the excess and the arithmetic verified band-by-band against §1, the billed amount is not supported by the contract.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Sagar Roadlines billed consignment SG-7003 (shipment SH-4229) above the amount produced by applying the §1 weight and distance components to the shipment's billed weight and distance, with no cold chain premium applicable since the shipment carries no special handling.
memo_narrative.why: The contract's freight formula in §1 (₹6/kg weight component plus ₹2/km distance component) accounts fully for the expected charge, and no other clause in the agreement (no accessorials, no applicable premiums under §3) explains the extra amount billed above that figure.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Request a corrected invoice from Sagar Roadlines for consignment SG-7003 citing §1, or ask the carrier to identify what charge accounts for the amount above the §1 formula if they believe it is owed.

adjudications.justification: The pricing trace correctly applies §1's formula: weight component (200 kg × ₹6/kg = 1200) plus distance component (140 km × ₹2/km = 280), for a contract-governed total of 1480. The cold chain premium in §3 correctly did not fire since the shipment record shows no cold_chain special handling. The shipment's distance_km (140) is the only distance figure on record for this consignment, and the rate card's own ambiguity note about 'booked lane distance' vs. actual distance does not present a genuine conflict here since no alternate distance value exists in the evidence. The billed amount exceeds this correctly-derived total by the stated delta, which is an unsupported overcharge under §1.

memo_narrative.what_happened: Sagar billed consignment SG-7009 above the amount that §1's weight-plus-distance formula produces from the shipment's recorded 200 kg weight and 140 km distance, with no cold chain premium applicable per §3.
memo_narrative.why: The pricing trace confirms the contract math (weight and distance components) ties out exactly to the lower figure, so the amount above is not supported by §1 or §3 and represents an overcharge.
memo_narrative.recommended_action: Send Sagar Roadlines a dispute referencing §1 and request a corrected invoice or credit note for consignment SG-7009 per §6.
